quarterly_data.signal: CEO Seamus Grady walked the capacity ladder to a single consolidated number: capacity right now is about $5.8 billion (the $5.3 billion Q4 exit run rate plus the Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion); Building 10 when fully available adds about $3.5 billion at the high end; Nava, the new factory in Nava Nakorn, adds about $250 million; and the newly acquired Santa Clara operation adds about another $250 million - which gets to $9.8 billion of capacity in calendar Q1, early in the March quarter, an 85% increase versus where the year ended. Beyond that, Building 11 - not yet announced - would take probably 18 months to build and add capacity for another $2.1 billion approximately, and the same for Building 12, so over the next three years Fabrinet could add another $4.2 billion on top of the $9.8 billion, taking it to approximately $14 billion of capacity. Even with all of that, Fabrinet is still looking for more land in Bangkok, in Thailand.
quarterly_data.figure: $5.8 billion now -> $9.8 billion capacity in calendar Q1 (an 85% increase); buildings 11 and 12 at about $2.1 billion each, 18 months each, to approximately $14 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Grady quantified the build-ahead economics of Building 10: it is about a 2 million sq ft factory costing about $132 million, $133 million for the building, and even if it were to sit idle the gross margin headwind is about 15 basis points, while just over five months' worth of operating profit at full run rate would pay for the whole factory. It will not sit idle - Fabrinet is already installing equipment and getting going on Floor 1 and will start to occupy Floor 3 in October. 'The downside risk is tiny and the upside opportunity is immense', with the real downside being that if the capacity is not put in place customers have to go somewhere else. Fit-out follows the customer: generic or standard equipment is paid for by Fabrinet, product-specific or unique equipment is paid for by the customer.
quarterly_data.figure: idle Building 10 gross margin headwind about 15 basis points; just over five months' worth of operating profit pays for the factory; building cost about $132 million, $133 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Csaba Sverha on funding the expansion: total CapEx for the last year was about $250 million and the company anticipates these elevated levels continue in fiscal 2027 in this $250 million range, covering the finishing of Building 10 and the fit-outs plus the Santa Clara facility that was just acquired for $76 million. Fabrinet took a small $75 million term loan signed with a Thai bank in August to finance growth in Thailand and is expanding credit lines, but is very comfortable with the balance sheet and comfortable financing growth from its own free cash flow rather than equity, because return on invested capital is close to the 40% mark. On the Q1 guide, the usual first-quarter merit salary increases add about 20, 30 basis point headwinds sequentially, which management expects to make up with efficiencies through the year.
quarterly_data.figure: CapEx about $250 million last year and in the $250 million range in fiscal 2027; Santa Clara acquired for $76 million; $75 million term loan; ROIC close to the 40% mark; Q1 seasonality 20, 30 basis point headwind

quarterly_data.signal: Datacom diversification status: Fabrinet is actually shipping to both hyperscale-direct and merchant transceiver manufacturers right now, and it is early days. The non-NVIDIA datacom customers are mostly initially 800 gig short reach transceivers and then moving to 1.6 in the future, with the initial foray at 800 gig. Grady reiterated Fabrinet will never become an ODM or own the IP - companies like Ciena, Cisco and Nokia would be deeply upset if it became a product company - and said Fabrinet has been picking up and winning business with some customers precisely because some competitors chose the ODM route. Management said it does not overly analyse share (customers do not always disclose it) and focuses instead on growing each opportunity to the multi-$100 million level where it can properly resource the customer. Beyond hyperscale, Fabrinet is also working with quantum compute customers that would fall into the new data center category, because moving those workloads around will need optics and not just electronics.

First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.
quarterly_data.figure: typical COGS about 70%-80% material, 20% value add

quarterly_data.signal: OCS ramp timing put on the clock for the first time: Fabrinet has shipped some OCS product but it is quite small today, and is working with a number of companies, one of whom it is actually shipping product to, while the others are early days and more startup-type companies. Management is looking forward to really beginning to ramp that over the next 12 to 18 months. On Coherent specifically, Grady said Coherent has a lot of its own in-house capacity at both the system level and the wafer level and does a lot of the in-house silicon itself, so he believes Coherent will continue to manufacture in-house. Fabrinet is happy to do sub-assemblies or the finished product, whatever the customer wants.
quarterly_data.figure: ramp over the next 12 to 18 months

contracts.signal: Grady described how the NVIDIA relationship has evolved: in the early days there was not any particular capacity out there for 400G and 800G transceivers in the volumes NVIDIA needed, NVIDIA acquired Mellanox and designed its own transceivers, and Fabrinet was the only manufacturer of their 400G and then 800G transceivers. NVIDIA has naturally diversified over the years and has multiple sources now for 800G transceivers, including its own design that Fabrinet makes but also other designs sourced from other suppliers. Management said this was always the plan, that NVIDIA remains a very important customer, and that the outsized early growth was always going to have to be replaced with growth in other areas.
